coherence.reasons: X's governing thought (firm levers reach ~2.6%, a prepared second wave closes to 3.0%) is carried consistently through the gap sizing, lever table, waterfall, covenant bridge, one-time budget and sensitivities; the numbers tie (7.7 + 30.1 = 37.8; wave 2 of 9.9). It has minor slips: slide 11's title says the plan 'reaches 3.0%' when firm levers give 2.6%, slide 10 calls promotions the 'largest single cause' although its own bridge puts e-commerce higher, and the target is quoted as both $45M and $42-43M on different sales bases. Y's storyline is clean and simple, but its governing thought of 'about 3.2% by FY2028' is contradicted by its own caveat: the 2027 wage rise it excludes would leave margin near 2.7%, below target. The title 'clearing the target before the 2027 wage rise' papers over that, since the rise lands inside FY2028. Y also names the wage rise 'the main risk' without building it into the answer, so its top-line claim does not follow from its own evidence.

judgment.reasons: Both reject the 8% cut and freeze, and both propose promotion pruning, delivery repricing, targeted labour, shrink protection and store exits, which matches the key's preferred recommendation. X weighs the trade-offs more fully. It compares three options, including click-and-collect-only as a fallback that needs the owners' consent. It stages the three vote-requiring stores behind a fix test and shows their 3.4-year payback. It haircuts the promotion gain by 25% for lost volume and keeps depth in ValuMart-exposed stores. It builds the known wage step into the baseline and admits the firm plan falls short, with a triggered second wave. It shows covenant headroom of about $5M and a one-time budget of $17M against the $25M cap. Y assumes the full 0.7 pp promotion recovery with no volume loss, and it folds all nine store exits into the base plan without weighing the $7.5M cost or payback. Its covenant case clears by only about $0.1M (15.3 + a quarter of 19.2). It defers costing against the $25M cap to a next step. Its plan only reaches 3.0% by leaving out a known cost headwind.

evidence.reasons: Both get the core calculations right: margins by year, the driver bridge (promotions -0.70, shrink -0.50, private label +0.18, e-commerce -0.84, labour -0.30), the e-commerce drag of -$10.4M, the fee test worth about $2.5M, and store exits of $6.6M / $4.4M. X goes further. It decomposes labour into a wage effect (+1.11 pts) and a productivity offset (-0.77 pts). It reconciles the e-commerce team's 6.1% to -$0.5M after delivery and then to -8.2% on incremental sales. It gives per-order economics for both channels with break-even incrementality. It tests the category team's claim quantitatively and flags it as correlation. It gives a range for shrink clawback ($3.8-7.5M) and labels its assumptions and allowances explicitly. Its weaker points are assumption-heavy sizing of vendor funding and unsourced one-time allowances, both flagged. Y's weaker inferences are more material. It attributes the entire 0.5 pp shrink rise to the fall in hours in order to project another 0.5 pp. It assumes sales moved off promotion stay at regular price with no volume loss. It dismisses the category claim only as 'sales, not profit'. It compares the management plan at 2.0% without the wage step. Its headline 3.2% omits the wage rise entirely.

revision.reasons: Both correctly revise management's wage-inflation hypothesis: labour is about 13% of the fall, hours per $1,000 fell 6%, and the leanest stores have the highest shrink. Both keep a targeted labour element rather than dropping labour entirely, and both reject the freeze. Y is fair in acknowledging that the wage rise is real ('as the CFO and COO say'). X is somewhat more rigorous. It quantifies how much of the wage rise productivity absorbed. It tests management's view explicitly as one of seven conditions. It re-costs the draft plan forward to FY2028 at about 1.1%, including the wage step and shrink. It also revises its own margin-first hypothesis when the levers prove insufficient. Y's revision is sound but less thoroughly tested, and it leaves the forward wage step outside the plan.

overall.reasons: X would serve the CEO better before the board and the lender. It rests on a quantified bridge and sizes every lever with ranges. It includes the known 2027 wage headwind and says honestly that the firm levers reach only about 2.6%. It then offers a concrete second wave and a fallback, with triggers. It shows covenant headroom and a one-time budget inside the cap, and it sets out sensitivities and specific board decisions. Y is concise, and its diagnosis is right, but its headline 3.2% depends on excluding a known $7.3M cost and on assuming no volume loss from the promotion cut. Its covenant case has almost no headroom, and the $25M capital constraint is left uncosted. Those gaps would leave the decision maker exposed on exactly the constraints the pack sets.
